mcqs.question: An image is purely decorative. What is the correct way to keep it out of screen-reader output?
options: Omit the alt attribute entirely
Use alt="decorative image"
Use an empty alt, alt=""
Give it role="img" and no alt attribute
mcqs.explanation: An intentionally empty alt tells assistive technology the image is decorative and can be skipped. The strongest distractor is option 0: a missing alt is not the same statement; it is unspecified, and screen readers may announce the filename or the image's presence, forcing users to guess. Option 1 announces the literal words 'decorative image', and option 3 creates an image with no name at all.

mcqs.question: A teammate adds maximum-scale=1, user-scalable=no to the viewport meta to stop unwanted zoom. What is the impact?
options: It is fine as long as desktop users can still zoom with browser controls
It improves accessibility by preventing accidental zoom
It can prevent pinch-zoom and text resizing, removing a primary low-vision strategy and conflicting with WCAG resize-text requirements
Browsers universally ignore it, so there is no effect
mcqs.explanation: Zoom is part of the accessible responsive experience, and blocking it takes away how many low-vision users read the page, conflicting with the ability to resize text. The usual motivation, iOS zooming into focused inputs, is better solved by giving inputs a 16px font size (https://css-tricks.com/16px-or-larger-text-prevents-ios-form-zoom). The strongest distractor is option 3: some modern browsers ignore the flag in some conditions, but plenty of browser and WebView combinations still honor it, so 'universally ignored' is false and dangerous.

mcqs.question: A page has a header navigation, a breadcrumb, and a footer navigation, all marked up as nav. How do you make them distinguishable for screen-reader users?
options: Give each repeated nav a distinguishing label, for example aria-label="Primary", "Breadcrumb", and "Footer"
Replace two of them with div elements so only one nav remains
Rely on the links inside each nav to explain the difference
Add an h2 inside each nav so the heading structure distinguishes them
mcqs.explanation: Repeated landmarks of the same type should carry distinguishing labels so the landmark list shows three different entries and users can jump straight to the one they need. The strongest distractor is option 1: removing nav semantics throws away free navigation structure instead of disambiguating it. Option 3 is a real half-measure: headings help heading-based navigation but do not label the landmarks themselves.

mcqs.question: A product-card image renders 320px wide on desktop and full-bleed on phones. The markup is . On a 1440px-wide viewport, what is wrong and what is the fix?
options: Nothing: after layout the browser measures the 320px card and fetches the matching candidate, so sizes only matters as a preload hint.
sizes describes a full-viewport slot, so the browser computes roughly 1440px and fetches a much larger file than the 320px card needs; state the real slot, e.g. sizes="(width <= 600px) 100vw, 320px".
Width descriptors in srcset must be ordered largest-first; otherwise the browser takes the first entry, here the 480w file.
Without x density descriptors the browser ignores srcset entirely and always downloads the src file.
mcqs.explanation: sizes is the declaration the browser uses to compute the rendered slot before it downloads anything, so 100vw tells it the image fills a 1440px viewport and it chooses a candidate for that width even though the card is 320px: the classic over-fetch. Declaring the real slot, with the last condition as the default, makes the selection match the layout (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Guides/Responsive_images). The strongest distractor is option 0: selection is driven by sizes, not by a post-layout measurement, which is precisely why the browser can start fetching early and why a wrong sizes keeps costing bytes. Option 3 confuses the implicit sizes fallback (100vw) with srcset being ignored, and x descriptors are for fixed-size slots rather than a requirement. Option 2 invents an ordering rule; the browser compares candidates by computed density, not by list position.

mcqs.question: A "your session expires in 60 seconds" prompt must block the page until the user answers. Which native construction actually does that?
options: A popover="manual" element: it stays open until explicitly dismissed, so it blocks interaction with the rest of the page.
A <dialog> element opened with show(), because opening a dialog is modal by definition.
A <dialog> element opened with showModal(): the rest of the page becomes inert, focus is kept inside, and Escape dismisses it.
A popover="auto" element plus aria-modal="true", so assistive technology treats the page as blocked.
mcqs.explanation: Modality comes from showModal(): it makes outside content inert, contains focus, renders a ::backdrop and supports Escape dismissal, which is exactly the must-answer-first requirement (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/dialog). The strongest distractor is option 0: manual only changes light-dismiss behavior (a manual popover does not close on outside clicks), but the Popover API is always non-modal, so the page stays fully interactive behind it. Option 1 uses show(), which opens non-modally with no backdrop and no inertness, and option 3 lies to assistive technology: aria-modal does not create inertness or focus containment, and an auto popover still light-dismisses on outside interaction (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Popover_API).

mcqs.question: A pricing table is written with <div> elements and CSS grid and matches the design pixel for pixel. What is lost for screen-reader users, and what is the right fix?
options: Only the visual affordances are missing; adding role="grid" to the wrapper is enough to expose it as a table.
Nothing structural: add tabindex="0" and an aria-label to every cell so users can tab through the values.

The divs expose no header-cell relationships, so figures are announced without their row and column context; use a native <table> with a <caption>, <th scope="col"> for the price columns and <th scope="row"> for the plan names.
Adding role="table" to the wrapper makes the browser infer rows and cells from the child divs.
mcqs.explanation: A native table is what creates the row and column header associations a screen reader announces while moving between cells, the caption names the table, and scope states each axis explicitly (https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/tables/). The strongest distractor is option 3: ARIA roles do not cascade, so a role="table" wrapper with plain div children exposes no rows, cells or headers; you would need role="row", role="columnheader" and role="cell" on every element and would still be re-owning table navigation, which is strictly worse than the native element. Option 0's role="grid" is an interactive, focus-managed widget pattern with its own keyboard contract, not a shortcut for read-only data, and option 1 turns a many-cell table into a tab-stop maze while aria-label expresses no relationships.

mcqs.question: A form posts to /profile with method="post". Without JavaScript, the Save button must submit to /profile/save and the Delete button to /profile/delete. Which markup works?
options: Set formtarget="/profile/delete" on the Delete button.
Nest a second form, <form action="/profile/delete" method="post">, inside the existing form around the Delete button.
Set action="/profile/delete" directly on the Delete <button>.
Give each submit button a formaction override: <button type="submit" formaction="/profile/delete">, plus formmethod if the method must change too.
mcqs.explanation: formaction is the per-button override for the form's processing URL, and its siblings formmethod, formenctype and formtarget override the other navigation attributes, so one form can reach different endpoints with zero JavaScript (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-control-infrastructure.html#form-submission-algorithm). The strongest distractor is option 0: formtarget is a real override, but it chooses the browsing context (_self, _blank), not the URL, so the POST still lands on /profile. Option 1 is invalid HTML because forms cannot be nested, so the inner form is ignored, and option 2 invents an action attribute on <button>: the button-level attribute is formaction, not action.

scenarios.prompt: At widths of 60rem and up, this page renders visually as Filters on the left, then Results, then Details. Describe exactly what (a) a screen-reader user reading linearly and (b) a keyboard-only user experience at that width, why it happens, and how you would fix it without changing the visual design.

code.code:
Result 1

Details

scenarios.modelAnswer: The DOM order is Results, Details, Filters, and neither screen-reader reading order nor sequential keyboard navigation follows grid placement; both follow the document. So at desktop widths a screen-reader user hears the results first, then the details, then finally the filters that scope them, and a keyboard user tabs into Result 1 before ever reaching the filter checkbox. Sighted users see Filters first, which is presumably the intended task flow, so the two audiences get different sequences and focus appears to jump around when compared with the visual layout. The fix is not CSS trickery and never positive tabindex: reorder the HTML source so the logical order is Filters, Results, Details, and keep the grid placement purely as the visual presentation of that order. Then test by reading the page and tabbing through every interactive element at each responsive layout, because the narrow layout must also make sense in the new source order.
rubric: States that reading order and tab order follow DOM source order, not grid-template-areas placement.
Describes the concrete mismatch: users hit Results and Details before the Filters that scope them.
Fixes the HTML source order and keeps grid placement as presentation only.
Rejects positive tabindex as a patch and can explain why (separate order, maintenance burden, does not fix reading order).
Mentions re-testing keyboard traversal and reading order at every breakpoint, including the narrow layout.

scenarios.prompt: This revenue table is built from divs and CSS grid so it matches the design. It looks correct, but a screen-reader user reports hearing "North 120k 135k South 98k 110k" with no idea which figure belongs to which quarter. (a) Name what is lost and why. (b) Rewrite the markup so the same visual result is accessible. (c) State what you would verify before shipping.

code.code:
Region
Q1
Q2
North
$120k
$135k
South
$98k
$110k

scenarios.modelAnswer:
(a) The divs are layout only: nothing in that markup exposes a table, a row, a cell or a header. The aria-label on the section names a region, not a table, so the accessibility tree holds a flat run of text. Two things are lost. First, header-cell associations: when focus reaches $135k there is no reason for the screen reader to say "Q2, North", and that context is exactly what a data table contributes. Second, table navigation: commands that move between cells or jump by row and column are unavailable, so a small grid becomes a linear read of numbers whose meaning depends on the visual position the user cannot see. (b) Use the native element for the semantics and keep the visuals in CSS:
Quarterly revenue by region
RegionQ1Q2
North$120k$135k
South$98k$110k
The caption names the table instead of assigning a name to a region, scope="col" states the column axis on the quarter headers and scope="row" states the row axis on the region names, and the figures stay in td. Reproduce the design with table CSS instead of going back to divs: table-layout: fixed plus a colgroup with column widths for the 2fr/1fr/1fr proportions, border-collapse for the rules, and padding and alignment for the cells. The point of the fix is to keep one source of truth: the element carries the relationships, the stylesheet carries the look. Do not paper over it with ARIA on divs either, because role="table" alone creates no rows, cells or headers, and building the full role set by hand means re-owning table navigation for no gain. (c) Verify with a real screen reader rather than only with an accessibility-tree inspector: confirm the table is announced with its caption and that each figure is announced together with its region and quarter. Then check the narrow viewport, where the table may need horizontal scrolling: the scrollable region has to be reachable and operable with the keyboard, and the visual result must still match the breakpoints the design specified. Finally, decide deliberately what happens on phones if the table is meant to collapse, instead of stripping the semantics to make it fit.
rubric: Identifies the root cause as missing table semantics (no rows, cells or header associations), not as a styling gap.
Rewrites with a native <table>, a <caption>, <th scope="col"> for the quarters and <th scope="row"> for the regions, with figures in <td>.
Keeps the visual result with table CSS (table-layout: fixed, colgroup widths, border-collapse, padding) instead of reverting to divs.
Rejects ARIA-only and tabindex fixes, explaining that role="table" does not cascade and a full row/cell/header role set would have to be hand-built.
Names concrete verification: screen-reader announcement of each cell with both headers, plus keyboard access and layout at narrow viewports.
